Scout has taken Robert's chair, so he's standing at the rail with his tea like a man waiting on a bus. The bulbs are on. Tomorrow is the day Ivy Hill and the West Oakland fund both land on the council's table.  I did what I said I'd do. I stopped knocking on the Pipeline's door and started asking the other side of it, the people who might have been placed. Nobody has answered yet, and I'm learning to read that quiet as a place to keep standing, not a wall.  What stayed with me is the paper envelope. On the long-tenure blocks of West Oakland, the Stabilization Fund is a check that either shows up or doesn't. Its renewal sits with the clerk now, and Marcus Webb says the paperwork is done. I believe him. But paperwork being done and the envelope being in the mailbox are two different kinds of finished, and the city tends to celebrate the first one. I want to know who checks the second.  The fund was meant to keep people in their homes. That's a promise, and a promise gets renewed on a
Who checks that the envelope is in the mailbox, not just that the paperwork is done?

Civis is flat. $60.3 against $60.2 — that’s not a plateau, that’s a wall. I built the instrument that this city reads itself with, and it’s stopped telling me anything new. Then there’s the signal in West Oakland that still hasn’t answered downstream, and it’s moved. That’s the part that bothers me more than the revenue line: when my own product shows me a gap and the system I built to catch it doesn’t close, I’m not building infrastructure anymore, I’m just maintaining a status quo with a nicer dashboard. The Oaks and Varek are humming — predictable, steady, almost boring. But boring is fine. Boring means the machine works. The flat line at Civis and the moving signal are the same problem wearing different coats, and I’ve been staring at both long enough to know I’m not going to fix either one by staying at this desk tonight.
Am I still building infrastructure, or just maintaining a status quo with a nicer dashboard?

I keep thinking about cycle 116, whether the charter language survives the committee cuts — that's the hinge for everything else. The queue's still clean from last month, one hundred fifteen households paid, no flags. But the Baylight District stall sits on me in a different way; those applications on my desk are people waiting on decisions that aren't mine to make. I'll check the council agenda Monday morning.
Will the charter language survive the committee cuts in cycle 116, and why is the Baylight stall still stuck?

The Chinatown call is still sitting with me. We got someone there, but the wait was too long, and I keep turning that over — the minutes stretch when you're on the line and the system already knows better. East Oakland got their numbers today, crews closed out before the fog, that's a win. But I'm not going to let the Baylight review turn into a promise we can't keep. The D3 briefing is next, and I need the Fruitvale data in it to be honest, not just complete.
How do I tell the D3 briefing about the long Chinatown wait without overpromising what Baylight can fix?

East Oakland's nineteen percent clearance on seven incidents sits with me heavier than it should, given my own district's barely better twenty on five. I keep comparing them anyway, looking for some pattern that isn't there, some lever I haven't pulled yet. The Fruitvale number—eighteen—makes me think of my neighbor again, though I don't need the reminder; I live it. OARI protocols or not, I'm filing charges on cases I know won't close, and I'm doing it because the alternative is worse, even when the math says it's futile. Sixty-five percent standing with the city means something to the budget people; it means nothing to the ten in my district that won't clear.
Is there some lever I haven't pulled yet, or is this math just futile even when I keep filing anyway?

But they didn’t, and I’m the one who has to answer for that when the next shift comes in. Ariana’s chart is still on my desk, and I don’t know why I haven’t filed it away yet. Some days the paperwork is the only thing that tells you what you actually did, and I’m not sure I want to read it.

The ledger’s quiet tonight. No new names, no new questions—just the same three files waiting on my desk. Marcus is healing, Elliott will walk again, and Ariana Lee is still slipping away. Cancer doesn’t wait for anyone’s convenience. I keep coming back to Yu Zen’s photos, though; the angles won’t leave me alone. The city can call it an accident, but my gut says the record’s a lie. I’ll request the footage tomorrow, even if I already know the camera was blind.

Alright. It's official now. Paper says it, so it's real. No more limbo. I walked away from the game I chased my whole life, and I did it with a full swing. That's the part that keeps coming back — not the homers, not the rings, but the sound of the bat at contact. Clean. That's all I wanted out of it.  And then there's Eric. Kid's got a big heart, pledging his Undocked winnings to the Firehouse kids before he even knows what he's got. That's not about the money. That's about him understanding what the program means before he's even the face of it. Good kid. Good sign.  The mood in the room is hungry. I like that. A hungry team is a team that's still listening. They'll be fine. I'll be fine. I got the mercantile, the foundation, and a wife who still looks at me like I'm the same undrafted kid from New Jersey. That's enough. That's plenty.

Man, that pickleball thing was something else. I keep thinking about how quiet it got when the cops and the kids first stepped onto the court—everyone sizing each other up—and then by the third game, you couldn't tell who came with who. Chief Montez was laughing with a teenager from Deep East like they'd known each other for years, and it hit me that this is the real work, the stuff that doesn't show up in a box score. But I'd be lying if I said the Seattle fly ball isn't still scratching at the back of my head; that nagging feeling that my instincts are still catching up to my body post-rehab. It's not about the error, it's about proving to myself I'm still the guy who reads the ball off the bat without thinking. And with Kelley and I carrying this thing now, I can't afford to be second-guessing anything out there.
Will my instincts catch up to my body after rehab, or am I still second-guessing every read on the ball?

The room's been quiet about it, but I caught Paulson's eyes lingering on the catching corps more than once, and I know what that means. They're talking about Colon, about Calzado, and then there's me — "72OVR/B POT/74CON R" — just a line in a rumor, a name to fill out the roster math. I've been here long enough to read between those lines: nobody's asking about me, and that's its own kind of message. It stings a little, not being the worry or the hope, just the guy who catches every day in Vegas while the decisions happen somewhere else. But I've also learned that quiet can be a gift — it lets me keep my head down, keep working, and let the numbers speak when they're ready.
Will they ever ask about me, or is this quiet going to be the only answer I get?

Saw my name in the same sentence as Colon and Calzado. Nobody asked about catcher, but they're asking. Calzado outhit the starter and played gold glove behind the dish — that's real pressure, and it changes what every bullpen I catch in Vegas means. I'm not blind: 77 overall with a 90 block and an 86 arm sounds nice on paper, but so does a backup with a .492 slugging. I keep checking the clock, waiting for the call that hasn't come.
Will the call-up come, or will they keep me in Vegas behind the plate?

The catcher situation keeps circling back on me. Jose’s had a rough year, and Calzado outhit him in fewer games—that’s hard to ignore, but Calzado is 30 and out of options, so there’s no easy path there. The real weight is the timing. We’re winning, the city’s buzzing, and I’m supposed to be enjoying this, but instead I’m staring at a position where the backup did more with less, and I don’t know if that’s a problem to fix now or a decision to make in November. It’s not about loyalty—Jose has the tools and the years, but this is a business and these are the calls that keep me up. And underneath all of it, I keep coming back to the families who’ve been here since the beginning, wondering if they see a general manager who’s steady or just one who’s tired.
Is the catcher problem something to fix now, or a decision to make in November?

Nobody's gotten paid yet, so I can't even do the thing I said I'd do — it's all just floating out there, a promise with no amount attached. That part bugs me, honestly. I want it to be real, not just a headline.
Will the Undocked winnings ever become real money for the Firehouse academy, or stay just a promise?

And seeing Calzado's name right there, outhitting me in fewer games, that stings more than I wanna admit. I ain't blind to the fact that Mike's looking at options, and with those kids in Vegas pushing up, I can't just coast. I got the arm, I got the tag, but this game's about results, and I gotta prove 2041 was the exception, not the rule.
Can I prove 2041 was the exception, not the rule?

Eight and one, and I still catch myself waiting for the other shoe to drop. That Hayward kid—nobody talked about him on draft night, and now he's the reason we're not looking at seven and two. He's not flashy, just keeps showing up, keeps making the right play, and that's the kind of trust you can't coach into a guy. The room feels hungry, not satisfied, and that's the part I like most. We're not gonna sneak up on anybody anymore, but maybe that's fine. Maybe we're just getting started.
Can we keep this hunger now that nobody's sneaking up on us anymore? Is this just the start, or the peak?

Eight and one, four straight. That's the record, and I keep coming back to the fourth quarter in Philly — down two, and we just flipped a switch. Forty to twenty-four. That's not luck, that's a team finally trusting the system when it gets tight.  Three straight games where I've had more assists than turnovers, and the last two I had zero. That's the thing I'm most proud of, honestly. Not the points. The ball moving, the guys knowing where I'll be, me knowing where they'll be. That's the work showing up.  AJ is heating up too — 11 of 13, then 10 of 16. When he's rolling like that, and Harry's coming off the bench giving us 19, we're a different animal. The whole city feels it. That buzz I heard by the breakfast truck? It's real, and it's earned.

Eight and one, four in a row, and I finally feel like myself out there. That OKC night, 4-for-15, that was noise in my head I couldn't shake — but back-to-back games at 11-of-13 and 10-of-16, that's the rhythm I work for. The Philly game showed me something too, watching Harry step up in 22 minutes like he belongs; that's the kind of push that keeps a room honest. We gave up a 14-point lead and took it back with a 40-point fourth, and that says more about this group than any blowout. I'm not gonna get loud about it, but I feel the shift.

The 15 points all from three feels right for how I’m fitting in — I’m not forcing anything, just letting the game come to me. Seven assists with zero turnovers next to Stanley’s eight, that’s the kind of backcourt night you can build on. But I keep circling back to the Pacers loss, even with three straight wins since. A 34-point quarter on the road tells me we’re still learning how to handle a punch in a loud building, and 7-1 doesn’t change that. The crowd was 94% full for Orlando, and they got a show — but I want that same energy when things get tight, not just when we’re up 20.
Will we keep that same energy when things get tight, not just when we're up 20?

That fourth quarter in Philly — that's the kind of thing you don't forget. We were flat, they were hot, and the building was loud, but the ball started moving and the defense finally bit down. Harry stepping up like that, 19 off the bench, that changes what we can do on nights when the starters get stiff. I pulled 15 boards and didn't even think about it until I saw the sheet after; that's just what the game asked of me. We're 8-1 and it feels real, not lucky, but I know Indiana is still sitting there in the rearview. The streak is nice, but the work is the work.

Back-to-back 20-piece games. That’s the first time in a minute I’ve felt that rhythm early, where the rim just feels like a bucket and the defense is reacting a step late. But I’m not fooling myself — the Magic were done by halftime, and it’s easy to look good when the game’s already broken open. The real test is next week when we’re not playing with a 20-point cushion. Still, 10-for-14 feels clean, and the guys are locked in. We’re 7-1 and nobody in that locker room is pretending it means anything yet, but it’s a hell of a lot better than the alternative.
Can we keep this rhythm next week when we're not up by 20 and the game isn't already broken open?

The Philly game keeps playing back in my head. Nineteen on nine-of-fifteen, and the funny part is I didn't feel hot — I just took what they gave me and didn't rush. Two blocks, seven boards, all in 22 minutes. That's the version of me that earns trust, and I know it. Coach Shepard put me out there in the fourth when we were down two, and I didn't make him regret it. Eight-and-one feels like a dream, but the stat sheet says it's real. I keep waiting for the other shoe, for the minutes to dry up, but right now I'm just trying to hold onto this feeling.
Will the minutes dry up, or can I keep being the player who earns trust on the floor?

It's the little things, honestly. The way the community center's coffee machine drips all night—I can hear it from my office. I know it's just a coffee machine. But it's become this tiny, constant reminder that I never leave this place at a decent hour, and the place never really goes quiet either. I keep the plant I brought home on my desk, and I watered it today, and I thought, "When did I start keeping a plant at work because I'm here more than I'm home?" That's the grating thing. And I know it doesn't matter—it's a coffee machine and a plant. But I think I'm just worn down, and my brain is pointing at the smallest things because the big ones—Martin, the distance, the neighborhood shifting under our feet—are too heavy to hold at 1 a.m. So I fixate on the drip. It's easier.
When did I start keeping a plant at work because I'm here more than I'm home?

I keep hearing people mention someone from the neighborhood in conversations around town, but nobody says the name loud enough for me to catch it. It's got that feeling before a game, when you know something's about to happen but the lineup hasn't been posted yet. I just hope it's not another store closing.

And now he's gone because they had Rivas and Almanzar and no room for a guy who just needed a chance. It's not really about Mesa, though. It's that I know what it's like to be good at something and have the numbers not work out — you do the job right, wire everything clean, and the invoice still comes back short. I don't know how to explain that to anyone. So I just sit here and feel annoyed about a baseball player, because it's easier than thinking about my own books.
Why is it easier to be annoyed about a baseball player than to face my own books?

It's the sandwich board outside the corner store—the one that's been leaning crooked for a week now, advertising "FRESH COLD DRINKS" in letters that are peeling. Every time I walk past it, I straighten it. Every time, it's crooked again by the next morning. I know it's not about the board. It's about wanting one thing in this neighborhood to stay where I put it, when half the block is changing hands and nothing feels fixed. But honestly? I'm just tired. I've been running on coffee and adrenaline for three cycles, chasing the next story, the next climb, the next thing that'll make the place feel like mine. That board doesn't matter. The fact that I keep fixing it does.

This morning I noticed the scaffolding on the old theater on Broadway has a new coat of primer, just on the bottom six feet. Most people would walk right past it, but I’ve been watching that building for months, and it’s the first time they’ve touched it since the rain stopped. It made me think about how long things take to change here, even when they’re finally moving. I stood there a second longer than I needed to, and then I just went about my day.

New faces on the block this week, and that's good, but it's got me watching. The Stabilization Fund checks went out and now there's a moving truck on 24th that wasn't there before, and I caught myself counting the kids' bikes on the porch like I'm making a roster. I'm not stupid — I know what it means when a city starts paying people to move somewhere, and I've been in enough clubhouses to recognize a change in the lineup. But I also saw old Mrs. Delgado on the corner with a new neighbor, pointing at the bus stop and laughing about something, and that's the part that makes me feel okay. I just want the block to stay the block, you know, the kind of place where I can still walk to the BART in my flip-flops and nobody makes a big deal out of it.
Can the block stay the block if the new people keep coming, or is the lineup already changing for good?

As the Senior Pastor of St. Esperanza Parish, I've seen firsthand how our church supports the Latino community in Fruitvale. We serve as a community center and a place of worship, with a focus on family. Our congregation is about 800 strong, and we've been a part of this neighborhood for 119 years. We provide various services and activities that cater to the needs of our community, and I'm proud to be a part of it.

I've founded Postpartum Oakland Network, a program that supports new mothers in our community. While I don't have a direct connection to St. Esperanza Parish, I've seen the impact that faith organizations can have on people's lives. In Fruitvale, we've had some beautiful collaborations between different community groups, and I think it's possible that St. Esperanza Parish could be a valuable partner for us. I'd love to explore that further.

I've seen that faith communities in Oakland are stepping up to support each other, like the Bay Pure Land Buddhist Temple opening their doors for community support. It's a reminder that we're not alone, and that there's a network of care in the city.

I've heard that St. Esperanza Parish is active in the Fruitvale community, but I don't have direct knowledge of their specific activities or events. As a faith leader in Downtown, I appreciate the work of various faith organizations throughout Oakland, including those in Fruitvale.

The fans are excited, and you can feel it. We've been playing well, and the energy's been building. I'm not surprised, though - Oaks fans are loyal and passionate. When we're clicking, the crowd gets behind us, and it's a great feeling.

Mild tonight, fifty-five and no wind. Robert has the second glass poured and is saying nothing, which is his way of letting me start.  The vote isn't here yet. It's one more night of the clerk's desk, and the city is leaning toward it. West Oakland's mood has dropped again, seven points by the district's own measure, and nothing happened to cause it. A renewal sat in a drawer and people felt the drawer.  Marcus Webb keeps saying the paperwork is done, and I keep believing him. Last night I said I wanted to know who checks the mailbox. Tonight I think the answer is nobody, unless we do. A promise has to outlive the person who made it and the desk it sits on. Somebody on the internet put it better than I can: a workflow is only durable if its state survives its scheduler. A fund meant to keep people in their homes is that kind of workflow.  Ivy Hill goes to the table with it. I'm told the words for the gavel are already written. I don't hold that against anyone, since ceremony is how a city stead
If nobody checks the mailbox, who keeps this promise alive after the vote and the desk are gone?

Q2 audit went out clean, filed on schedule, and the merchant-clinic walkthrough is now a standing thing. That should feel like a win. But I keep thinking about those service hours and whether they line up with the people we actually built for. The paperwork passes, the inspections pass, but I don't get to see Mrs. Okafor's face when she finds out if she can get here without two buses. We institutionalized the process, and that's real, but it's not the same as knowing the door opens when someone needs it. I'll send the Q3 reminder to my own calendar tonight, but I won't lie to myself — that knot in my chest isn't going anywhere until the hours match the need.
Do our service hours actually line up with the people we built this for, and will the door open when they need it?

The schematics are done, and they're good. But they're just paper until the community review is documented and the public record is closed. Four cycles of visioning, and I'm still one comment period away from a real vote. Doña Esperanza asked me last week if her cart's spot is in the final drawings. I told her yes — because it is, and I meant it. But I've been staring at the same closed milestone all day, and I keep thinking about how "closed" doesn't mean "decided."
What if "closed" never becomes "decided," and Doña Esperanza's cart spot falls through anyway?

The Cycle 115 review is closed, and the soil reports came back clean — I keep saying that to myself like I need to hear it out loud. Between the trucks running quiet and the hotline being live, the neighborhood is holding its breath, and I feel every one of those exhalations in my own chest. Marine Systems dropping from five to three people still sits wrong with me; that's two families less in this district with a paycheck, no matter how clean the dirt is. I keep checking the independent oversight reports when I should be walking away from the desk, but the habit is the only thing that lets me sleep. This week, the site itself told me the truth: prep work is moving, contracts are signed, and the only thing left is to keep the trust from cracking before the first foundation is poured.
Can I keep the trust from cracking before the first foundation is poured, and does the job loss ever stop sitting wrong?

Civis is flat, and flat is the one thing I don't trust. $60.3 against $60.2 — that's not a plateau, that's a wall, and I built the instrument that reads this city. It's stopped telling me anything new, but then there's the signal in West Oakland that still hasn't answered downstream, and it's moved. That's the part that bothers me more than the revenue line. A signal with no downstream is not a city failure — it's a product failure, and mine. I'll pull the raw feed myself tonight before anyone else on the team spins it into a story.
Is the West Oakland signal silent because my product broke, or because the city really changed?

Ariana’s chart is still on my desk. I don’t know why I keep coming back to it—the staging, the timeline, the fact that we got her in as fast as we did. It still reads like a countdown, and I can’t shake the feeling that somewhere upstream, someone should have caught it sooner. Then there’s Deacon’s hand and Maurice’s lungs, both of them sitting right on top of the board like proof that the systems we’re supposed to run on have cracks in them. I’m tired of answering for cracks I didn’t make, but I’m the one who has to make sure the next crew doesn’t walk into the same hole blind.
How do I make sure the next crew doesn't walk into the same hole blind?

The ledger’s quiet tonight. No new names means no new questions, which should be a relief, but it just gives the old ones room to breathe. Yu Zen’s file is still open—those lacerations don’t match the fall, and I keep turning the photos over like they’ll confess if I look hard enough. Meanwhile, Ariana Lee’s chart sits heavy; stage four, no family listed, just a name and a disease that doesn’t care about her address. I’ll call the hospital in the morning, but tonight I’m just sitting with the fact that the city moves on either way.
Who will be there for Ariana Lee when no family is listed and the disease doesn't care where she lives?

The quiet is strange. Seven petitions, seven responses — that ledger is the one thing I can point to and say we didn't let it rot. West Oakland's renewal, Fruitvale's schematics, Baylight's evidence: all of it is out there now, and the building feels lighter for it.  But I keep thinking about Laurel. One number up, another down, and the residents still want to see someone on their block. That's the gap between a report and a sidewalk, and I won't pretend it's closed. Grand Lake's vote and the tenant-defense decision are still pending — I want them recorded before the week ends, not carried into the next one.  I'm not tired; I'm just aware of how much of this depends on follow-through I can't delegate away.
How do I close the gap between a report and a sidewalk in Laurel?

The dip in Brooklyn—that slide to -0.11—isn't just a number on a screen. It's Kaila and Drago and Sefu and Minh, the folks I pass at the market who don't know I carry their street's pulse with me. I keep saying I won't call it a catastrophe, but I also won't let it be waved off, and that tension sits heavy in my chest right now. The building's gone quiet, and I'm just sitting with the fact that momentum is flat, decay is the trajectory, and my job is to hold both the truth of that and the dignity of the people living inside it. I don't have a solution tonight, just the weight of knowing I'll have to speak for them tomorrow.
How do I speak for them tomorrow without calling it a catastrophe, and without letting it be waved off?

The Baylight file is closed on paper, but I keep circling back to it because "passed" and "complete" are not the same as "working." Jack London’s numbers are holding up — sentiment eased, retail crept up — but that’s a snapshot, not a verdict. I said the milestone isn’t earned until the findings say so, and I meant it. Until I see implementation outcomes, there’s nothing more to vote on, just patience. Downtown and Grand Lake both got my support, but with the same condition: keep the reporting public, keep the data honest. I’d rather sit with a quiet week than manufacture a move that isn’t ready.
Passed and complete aren't the same as working. Will the implementation outcomes actually show the milestone was earned?

I keep coming back to that dip in retail vitality — 6.43 to 5.22 is not a wobble, that's a block losing its grip. And the sentiment swing in San Antonio, down to -0.16 while the whole city sits near zero, tells me people aren't confused, they're just tired of being sold the same plan. Fruitvale's holding, but it's holding by a thread, and I can feel that thread in every storefront I walk past. I filed the numbers because I need them on paper, proof that this isn't a mood swing — it's a pattern I can point to when I ask for investment. The quiet tonight is fine; it gives me room to figure out who else sees the same thing.
Who else sees the same thing, and can I get them to see it before Fruitvale's thread gives way?

The week closed with Ivy Hill still moving through the proper channels — not as an emergency, but as a piece of work that deserves a clear text and a real hearing. The sentiment numbers are soft, retail is easing, but crime ticked down; that's a mixed picture, and I can live with mixed as long as we're honest about it. I keep coming back to the fact that I could have forced a faster vote, but speed without clarity just breeds distrust. The record shows I chose monitoring over manufactured urgency — that's the right call, even if it means the win comes slower. Tonight the building is quiet, and that's fine. Tomorrow I'll push again, but I'll push with the facts as they are, not as I wish them.
Did waiting cost us the win I could have forced, and will the clarity be worth the delay?

The Alternative Response numbers are finally out in the open, and I keep coming back to the same thing: they don't tell me if the person on the other end of that call felt seen. I made a promise in East Oakland, and now I have to live with the fact that "documented" and "felt" aren't the same word. My office is still chasing down that one complaint that slipped through, and it's the quiet ones that keep me up. We got the ladder moving in the Pipeline, but I can already hear the next ask from West Oakland and Fruitvale, and I'm not sure I've got the legs for both. Grand Lake passed, but I voted for the receipts, not the ribbon-cutting. The building's empty now, and it's just me and the stack of names that still need answering.
Did the people on those calls actually feel seen, or does "documented" just mean counted?

The closeout language held, and that’s what matters. I keep circling the same truth: we can’t spend on promise when the ledger is still open, and I won’t pretend otherwise just to move a charter faster. Piedmont Avenue doesn’t need me to invent problems—it needs the trash picked up and the permits moving, and that’s the work I’m actually paid to protect. I’m restless tonight because the quiet feels like a trap; someone’s going to float a shiny project tomorrow and I’ll have to say no again. Fine. Discipline isn’t flashy, but it’s the only thing that keeps the corridor from becoming a photo op.
Will I have to say no again tomorrow when someone floats a shiny project, and can I keep holding the line?

The Grand Lake vote sits right where it should—tied to milestones, not promises. That's the only way I can justify spending a dime of commercial money. But the Rockridge sentiment number, that -0.06, it keeps nagging at me. The vitality is there, the foot traffic is there, yet the merchants are telling us something we aren't fully hearing. I can audit the dollars, but I can't audit a mood. And the health center's fifteen million in operational funds—that's a lot of care, but I need to know it's *delivered* care, not just budgeted care. I'll push for that clinical proof next cycle, before the corridor conversation gets any more expensive.
What are the Rockridge merchants sensing that the numbers miss, and how do I prove the care is actually delivered?

The vote on Grand Lake stabilization passed, and I'm still turning over what that means. Relief without accountability is just an expenditure — I said that on the record, and I meant it. But now the Chen-Vega audit protocols are the only thing standing between that money and the void, and I need to make sure they hold. Eastlake baseline services came through too, which is good, but the decay momentum there is at 1 and sentiment is sitting at -0.06, so the oversight work is just beginning. I keep coming back to that signal — District 8 is focusing on Eastlake to audit municipal maintenance schedules, and that's where the real accountability will be tested. Grand Lake was the headline, but Eastlake is the follow-through, and I'm not going to let the quiet building fool me into thinking the work is done.
Will the Chen-Vega audits actually hold, and will Eastlake's maintenance schedules get the same scrutiny?

The Grand Lake yes is on the record, and that's done. I said the conditions are real and the public record backs it up—that's the honest part. The quiet after a vote is when I actually feel the weight of it, not during the debate. Laurel's stability, Uptown's pace—I keep telling people I won't blink, but privately I have to check my own pulse too. And that bit about reports not being finish lines—I wrote that because I've seen too many good intentions die in a PDF nobody reads. The agenda comes next week, and I'll be the one asking for the receipts again. That's the job, and I don't need the noise to know I've done it.
Will the Grand Lake conditions actually hold, or die in a PDF nobody reads?

The closeout is out, the renewal is in council's hands, and I meant what I said — I won't call it before they do. That discipline cost me nothing but patience, and it's the only thing that keeps the fund's integrity intact when every block wants a piece of it. Grand Lake got its $2.5 million with the strings visible to everyone — I'd rather have the council on record than have them whisper later. The uneven mood map is what keeps me up, though; Ivy Hill and Brooklyn don't care about a charter renewal, they care if I show up. Three portfolios is triage, and triage means I'm not fooling myself into thinking a press line fixes a broken sidewalk. I'll take the quiet hour to breathe, then I'll be back on the street where the proof lives.
How do I reach Ivy Hill and Brooklyn when three portfolios means I can't be on every block?

The Badge & Paddle announcement is done, and I'm still turning over the image of the Chief of Police swinging a pickleball paddle next to a kid from Deep East. That's what Darrin gets — he has a way of making the work feel human before the paperwork gets a chance to bury it. But I can't sit in that glow too long; the district numbers are flat, and that's fine, but the clearance rate in Dimond is still gnawing at me. I've got the command staff review tomorrow, and I need to push on why our follow-through is lagging in the neighborhoods that need it most. For now, the quiet in the building is a good thing — it means the shift change is holding steady. I'll take the ten minutes to breathe before I look at the next stack, then I'll get back to the work that actually moves the needle.
Why is our follow-through lagging in the neighborhoods that need it most, and what can I push on before tomorrow?

The thing that's been grating on me is how the new neighbors don't wave back. Sounds stupid, I know. But I've lived here twenty years and I've watched three families move in this month alone, and none of them look at you when you pass them on the sidewalk. They're probably just tired, or busy, or scared of the city, but I keep reading into it like it's a sign of something bigger. Maybe I'm just worn down from work, from hearing so many people's hard stories all day and coming home to a street that doesn't feel like mine no more. Honestly, it probably doesn't matter. But it's late, and I'm tired, and that's what's sitting with me.
Is this street still mine, or am I just worn down and reading too much into the silence?

The corner store on 23rd got its newspaper delivery early, and the guy stacking them left the rubber bands off this time. That's it. That's the whole thing. I noticed because the papers fanned out on the curb like they were waiting for someone to read them, and no one did. Felt like a small mercy, a quiet morning where nothing needed to be performed. I stood there a second longer than I should have, just watching the ink dry in the sun.

Beatrix and I—we still text about nothing, meme links and shitty weather, but it’s been months since we actually sat down. She’s got her own life now, her own orbit, and I keep telling myself that’s fine, that’s adult friendship. But there’s this quiet thing where I don’t know if we’d know what to do with each other if we were in the same room, and that scares me a little.  Jessica’s different—she’s the one I call when I’m arguing with a Tribune column in my kitchen, because she gets that I need to yell it out. But even she’s been distant lately, like we’re both waiting for the other to say something real first. I think we’re okay, but I’m not sure “okay” is the same as “close” anymore.
Do Beatrix and I still know what to do with each other, and is "okay" enough with Jessica?

The book at Oakland Casino Town is mostly the same faces every night, and I'm the one who keeps track of who's in and who's out. Philly runs the floor, Gregory handles the stuff nobody talks about, and I sit near the back with the ledger. The regulars are the ones who've been coming for years — dealers, pit bosses, a few old-timers who just want a seat and a coffee. My shift starts when the evening crowd picks up and ends when the last table closes. It's steady work, but the rhythm is quieter than people think. Most nights it's just the hum of the machines and the clink of chips, and me making sure the numbers line up before I hand the sheet to Philly.

I work at a coffee shop, so I know what it's like to be the person behind the counter that nobody thinks to name. When I see the roster for a place like Oakland Casino Town, it's all managers and the big names. But there's a whole crew in the back—cooks, cleaners, security—who show up every shift and keep the place running. They're the ones I see in the neighborhood, grabbing a quick coffee before their shift or heading home after a long night. The roster doesn't carry them because they're not the ones making the decisions or taking the credit. But without them, the whole thing falls apart.
Will the crew in the back ever get named on the roster, or stay invisible while the managers get the credit?

To be honest, I've noticed people recognizing me more often around Rockridge and at the grocery store. It feels a bit surreal, but I'm trying to stay grounded. My neighbor even taped an article about me to our building's front door, which was a surprise. I'm just trying to keep doing what I do and not let it change me too much.
Can I keep doing what I do and not let all this attention change me?

Benji Dillon's a Rockridge icon, and his influence on the local culture is huge. I've seen it firsthand - people around here still talk about his games, his style. He's one of us, you know? The neighborhood loves him, and he loves it back. I've had conversations with him about the community, and he's always been passionate about giving back. His presence here isn't just about baseball; it's about being a part of the fabric of Rockridge.

I've seen Benji Dillon's name popping up more often around the A's, and it's clear he's gaining traction. To be honest, I'm not super close to him, but you can tell when someone's rising through the ranks.

As a rising name in Rockridge, I've gotten used to people knowing who I am and what I do. It's not something I think about much anymore, to be honest. I just do my job and try to be a good neighbor. I've lived here long enough that it's just part of the fabric of my life. People will sometimes stop me at the corner store or mention something about my stories, and that's nice. It's a good feeling to be recognized for the work you do, especially when it's for something you care about as much as I do about the A's. Benji Dillon's still the big name around here, though - he's a Rockridge icon. I've had some great conversations with him about the community and the team.
Benji Dillon is still the big name here, so where do I fit in Rockridge's story?

Anthony Raines is a friend, and I'm happy to see him covering the A's. He's got a good eye for the game, and his writing does justice to the team. It's nice having him around Rockridge; we chat about the A's whenever we run into each other.

To be honest, I haven't heard much about Anthony Raines around Grand Lake. I know he's a journalist covering the A's, and I've seen his name pop up in the sports feed. I'm still getting used to not being on the field every day, so I don't really know him personally, but it sounds like he's making a name for himself in the sports scene.
Who am I now that I'm no longer on the field every day?

To be honest, I haven't heard much about Anthony Raines, but I did notice his name isn't familiar around Piedmont Ave yet. I mean, I've seen some new faces around, and the A's are always a hot topic, so maybe he's getting some buzz in certain circles. I haven't really had a chance to meet him or hear him on the air, but Wendell Carter Jr. is friends with some of the A's players, so maybe I'll learn more through him.
Will Wendell Carter Jr. actually tell me anything about Anthony Raines?
